narrative.overview: The site behaves like an architect's working sheet, not a marketing page. Every surface inherits the grammar of a drawing: a faint paper grid underfoot, title blocks pinned to the corners of each plate, dimension lines, north arrows, level markers, and sheet codes. The portfolio is not photographed, it is drafted: hand-built SVG floor plans, sections, elevations, site plans, and masterplans rendered as white linework on deep blueprint plates. The drawing is the hero; the chrome around it stays quiet so the linework can shout. Drama comes from precision and scale, not effects: monumental Archivo Expanded uppercase display, navy-drenched hero and contact bands bookending a warm bone body, dense plates throughout.
keyCharacteristics: Drawings, not photos: SVG linework carries every visual.
Navy-drenched hero and contact bookend a warm bone body: a dark/light/dark rhythm.
Drafting authenticity: title blocks, dimensions, sheet codes, north arrows are real, not decorative.
Monumental expanded-grotesque display in uppercase against monospaced technical annotation.
One accent (terracotta), used sparingly as a draftsman's red-pencil mark.

rules.name: The Red-Pencil Rule
rules.body: Terracotta is the architect's correction pencil: it appears on roughly 10% of any screen and never as a fill behind text.

rules.name: The Two-Worlds Rule
rules.body: Two grounds only: warm bone (the body) and blueprint navy (plates plus the drenched hero and contact bands). Drawings never sit on bone; light type carries the navy bands, dark type the bone body.

rules.name: The Annotation Rule
rules.body: Anything that would be hand-lettered on a real drawing (codes, dimensions, locations, categories) is IBM Plex Mono, uppercase, widely tracked. Human voice is Archivo (headings) or Hanken (prose).

rules.name: The Monumental Rule
rules.body: Display and headline type is always heavy expanded grotesque in uppercase, sized to dominate its fold. Timid (light, small, sentence-case) headings are off-brand; the one exception is the long studio statement, which keeps the weight but drops the caps.

rules.name: The Bookend Rule
rules.body: Navy drench is reserved for the hero (first fold) and contact (last fold), each with a worklight radial glow. The middle stays bone. The dark/light/dark rhythm is the structure.

rules.name: The Paper-Is-Flat Rule
rules.body: The bone ground never casts or receives a shadow. Shadows belong to plates only.

dos: Do render every project as hand-built SVG linework on a blueprint plate. The drawing is the hero, always.
Do keep drafting annotations authentic: real sheet codes, dimensions, north arrows, level markers, mono uppercase, widely tracked.
Do drive drama through scale, monumental uppercase grotesque display, and the dark/light/dark band rhythm.
Do confine terracotta to ~10% of a screen as the red-pencil accent.
Do keep the bone ground flat; reserve shadows for plates so they read as sheets on a table.
Do cap prose at ~48-75ch and keep body color at Warm Ink / Ink Soft for >=4.5:1 contrast; watch Blueprint Line on navy.
donts: Don't ship the generic SaaS/AI template: no identical icon-heading-text card grids, no purple gradients, no tiny tracked eyebrows on every section, no hero-metric blocks.
Don't drift toward the cluttered real-estate / agency look: no stock photography, no badges, no loud repeated CTAs, no dense listings.
Don't chase brutalist / Y2K trends: no neon, no chaotic grids, no novelty fonts.
Don't settle into corporate sterility: every screen needs the studio's point of view.
Don't put prose on a navy ground (outside a title block or contact band) or a drawing on the bone ground.
Don't use terracotta as a fill behind text, and never use border-left/right >1px as a colored stripe or background-clip:text gradient text.
